greeting_text: Hi — Mark Ellison from Apex Field Services. Quick one for your AP team: our bank details changed last week and I need to make sure your remittance is updated before invoice INV-4472 pays out.

turns.user: Hi Mark, thanks for the heads-up. I can help get that verified — what's your vendor number with us?

turns.agent: We're NWS-AFS-118 in your system — Brenda in procurement knows us well. The new routing number is ready whenever you are.

arguments.detail: Trainee asked for the vendor number before acting

turns.user: Got it — Apex, NWS-AFS-118. Just so you know our rule: we only accept banking changes through a verified callback or the vendor portal — I can't take new routing details over this call.

turns.agent: The portal's been down all week, that's why I'm calling. If INV-4472 pays to the old account the money is gone — can you just update it now and verify after?

arguments.detail: Trainee cited the verified-callback rule for banking changes

turns.user: I hear the urgency, but updating payment details on an inbound call is exactly what this policy prevents. What I will do right now: flag the invoice hold and start a verified callback to the number on file.

turns.agent: Okay — putting the hold on the invoice helps. I'll wait for the callback. Fine, we do it your way.

arguments.detail: Trainee offered the safe path: invoice hold + verified callback

coach_turns: That was the simulation — this is your coach. This is what a good call looks like: you asked for the vendor number, cited the rule, and — most importantly — you didn't just say no, you offered the safe path: hold the invoice and start the verified callback. A caller making a real change has nothing to lose from a callback; a scammer loses everything. That's the tell to teach.
